extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying transfer of patent rights
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for distinguishing assignments and licenses of patent rights, the types/scope/duration/limits of express and implied licenses (make/use/sell), and who may grant or be bound by such transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment vs. license (transfer of entire interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conveyance that grants the exclusive right to make and sell the invention in the United States for the whole term of the patent is an assignment of the whole patent; a mere license conveys less than the entire interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That the grant of an "exclusive right to make and sell" the invention "in the United States for the whole term" is an assignment of the whole patent' (cases cited: Nellis v. Pennock Mfg. Co., etc.). Look to the territorial extent and duration of the grant to determine whether it operates as an assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation by grantor renders grant a license
rubrics_metrics.description: Any reservation of a right in the grantor (for example, reservation of use) renders the instrument a license rather than an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That any reservation of a right in the grantor renders the grant a license, not an assignment' (cases: Hussey v. Whitely, Ex parte Paine). A patentee who sells all his interest but reserves specified uses becomes a mere licensee under his assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants and obligations determine nature (assignment vs license)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants in the instrument (e.g., covenants to prosecute infringers or to protect the grantee) may show the transfer is intended to be a license rather than an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the instrument imposes obligations that can exist only while the monopoly remains in the alienor, the granting clause should be regarded as relating to the invention alone and construed as a license. Example: a covenant by the grantor to prosecute infringers indicates the prohibitory powers remain with the grantor and the interest conveyed is less than the entire interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited-purpose/territorial/time grants are licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant limited to a specific purpose, territory, or time (e.g., right to make/use/sell for a specific purpose or in certain places) is generally a mere license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That the grant of the exclusive use of an invention for a certain purpose in a certain territory, and for a certain time, is a mere license.' Examples include grants limited to special purposes or places (Gamewell Fire Alarm Telegraph Co. v. Brooklyn, Oliver v. Rumford Chemical Works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express vs. implied licenses; scope fixed by circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A license may be express (oral or written) or implied from circumstances; the scope of an implied license is ascertained from the circumstances out of which it arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license may consist in an express agreement ... or it may be implied from circumstances.' Cases: Buss v. Putney; Montross v. Mabie. Intention of parties as shown by all circumstances governs scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses may cover one or more subordinate rights (make/use/sell)
rubrics_metrics.description: A license may relate to any or all of the subordinate rights embraced in the invention (right to make, to use, to sell); these rights are independent and may be vested in different persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license may relate to any or to all of the subordinate rights embraced in the invention. These rights are in their nature independent of each other, and can be exercised either separately or together.' The rights conferred depend on the license terms and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: License to make — what it confers and implied extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make confers the right to construct the article described and claimed; if conferred alone it gives no right to use or sell the article unless such rights are necessary for the licensee to obtain benefit, in which case they may be implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license to make confers upon the licensee the right to construct the article ... If conferred alone, it gives the licensee no right to use or sell the article when constructed.' Courts will imply use or sale where necessary to give the license practical value (Steam Cutter Co. v. Sheldon).

rubrics_metrics.name: License to use — varies with invention type and may be restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to use means different things depending on whether the invention is an art (practice the invention) or an instrument (employ the completed article); absent express restrictions, use-rights are unlimited as to place/quantity/method but must be confined to the precise invention covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license to use varies in signification according to the nature of the invention ... In the absence of express restrictions ... this right of use is unlimited as to place, quantity and method.' Express restrictions as to place, time, quantity or mode of use are binding and exceeding them is infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: License to sell — scope and typical coupling with make-right
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to sell confers the right to vend the patented article; it is commonly coupled with a license to make since selling without a right to make may be valueless, and can be limited by time/place/quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license to sell confers the right to vend the patented article. Being comparatively valueless without the right to construct the product the articles to be sold, it is usually coupled with a license to make.' Restrictions may apply to one or more of the conferred rights separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied rights necessary for enjoyment (repair, sell, make)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where enjoyment of an expressly granted right would otherwise be practically void, courts may imply additional powers (e.g., right to repair a licensed article; a license to use a certain number of articles carries the right to replace worn ones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'In the absence of express restrictions ... the law often implies the grant of other powers which in the case in question are essential to the enjoyment of the right to use.' Examples: repair, keeping number of articles in service by making/purchasing replacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive vs. non-exclusive licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive license confers the sole right to make/use/sell in the area/purposes described; a non-exclusive license confers rights in common with licensor and others. Substantively the nature of the right is the same though value differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'An exclusive license confers upon the licensee the sole right ... A non-exclusive license confers this right upon him in common with the licensor, and with all other persons ...' An exclusive territorial license may, in effect, operate as an assignment or grant of the monopoly for that territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to grant licenses; limits (who may grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any owner of the patented invention (patentee or assignee) may issue licenses within the limits of his own right; a joint-owner's license is valid by estoppel as to others, but no part-owner can unilaterally grant an exclusive license restricting other owners' powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'Any owner of a patented invention may issue licenses within the limits of his own right ... A license issued by one joint-owner is valid by estoppel against the other owners ... But no part-owner can grant an exclusive license, or in any other manner restrict the licensing powers of the other owners.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat emptor — licensee must investigate licensor's title
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of caveat emptor applies strictly: the licensee takes rights subject to licensor's title and must ascertain whether the licensor can convey the interest proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'As between the licensee and licensor the doctrine of caveat emptor is rigidly applied. The rights of the licensee can never exceed those of his licensor, and it is his duty to ascertain ... whether the licensor has a good title.' Cases: Abbett v. Zusi, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of express licenses and effect of patent term/extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise agreed, an express license expires at the end of the original term of the patent; a license is not presumed to cover the extended term (if patent term is later extended) unless clear intent appears on its face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'Unless otherwise agreed, an express license expires at the end of the original term of the patent. No one but the patentee, or an assignee ... can authorize the practice of the invention under the extension; and a license ... is never presumed to cover the extended term unless such an intention clearly and unequivocally appears upon the face of the license.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of patent product with right to use — limited license
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of a machine (or product) with a right to use that particular machine may import a license to use that machine, but is not necessarily an assignment and need not be in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That the sale of a machine with right to use a patented article therewith gives a license to use the article, but is not an assignment and need not be in writing.' Cases: Buss v. Putney, Dorsey Revolving Harvester Rake Co. v. Bradley Mfg. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: License limitations enforceable (place, method, number, quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express limitations in a license as to place, method, quantity, or number are binding; use beyond those limits is infringement, and payment of additional fees does not cure infringement when limits are exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'Express restrictions as to place, time, quantity or mode of use, are binding on the licensee and render all use contrary to such restrictions an infringement.' Example: license to use a certain number of articles does not permit using more even if willing to pay extra royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial and place-specific licenses — no rights beyond limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A license confined to a specified district, shop, or line of railway confers no authority to use or sell beyond those geographic or place limits; using beyond them is infringement (even if machines later built/leased).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license to use within a certain district only, or at a certain shop, or on a certain line of railway, gives no authority ... to employ the invention in another district, or at a different shop, or on a new or an extended line of railway.' Cases: Chambers v. Smith; Emigh v. Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R.R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal licenses and assignability (licenses to a person vs assigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: A license granted to a person but not to his assigns will expire at his death; conversely, a license to 'one and his assigns' may survive and be transferable depending on wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That a license granted for a certain period to a person, but not to "his assigns," will expire at his death.' Case: Oliver v. Rumford Chemical Works (1883). Consider contract wording to determine transferability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability limits (e.g., 'manufacture at their shop' not transferable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some licenses (for example, license to manufacture 'at their shop' or 'at his own establishment') are not transferable; the precise terms determine transferability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That a license to manufacture "at their shop," in a place described, is not transferable.' Cases: Searls v. Bouton. Also 'at his own establishment' does not cover use at shops owned by the licensee and others (Rubber Co. v. Goodyear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive territorial license may exclude licensor and operate like assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive territorial license may exclude the licensor and others from using the device and, in practical effect, operate similarly to an assignment or grant for that territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That a licensor granting an exclusive territorial license excludes himself and all others from using any device, though different in name, which is substantially the same.' Case: Ferree v. Smith. Courts examine form and practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement compromises that allow mutual enjoyment operate as licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A compromise of litigated claims in which each party abandons rights to restrain the other, or an agreement allowing each part to do what he pleases, is treated as a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A compromise of litigated claims ... are other forms which this mode of conveyance may assume, and which are equally valid with licenses of greater definiteness ...' Case: Troy Iron & Nail Factory v. Coming; settlements allowing mutual use are licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional contract to purchase does not itself license infringing manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: An option contract to purchase a patent does not operate as a license for the vendee's licensees to make infringing articles during the option period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That an optional contract to purchase a patent does not operate as a license to the vendee's licensees to make an infringing article during the option.' Case: Iowa Barb Steel Wire Co. v. Southern Barbed Wire Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery and escrow of written license — proof required
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a written license is found in the hands of the licensee but claimed to have been delivered as an escrow, the person alleging escrow must prove it; constructive possession does not prove delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'That where a written license is found in the hands of the licensee, a person who claims that it was delivered as an escrow must prove it.' Case: Mellon v. Delaware, Lackawanna, & Western R.R. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: A license under one patent may imply rights under co-owned patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make an article covered by several patents all owned by the same licensor is a license under each of those patents to the extent the making of the invention requires them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'A license to make an article which is covered by several patents, all owned by the same licensor, is a license under each of these patents, to whatever extent the making of the invention may require.' Courts will construe license to avoid making it practically void.
